To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

early androgen-induced programs in the prostate embryo recapitulate the molecular signature of prostate cancer, and that this recapitulation is most evident in aggressive, lethal forms of prostate disease.

androgen exposure during prostate development regulates a program of gene expression in the epithelial buds that is similar to that in prostate cancer, and that this program is associated with prostate cancer progression and metastasis.
androgen exposure in the prostate during embryonic development regulates a gene expression program that includes many genes and functional pathways previously implicated in prostate cancer.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of microRNAs in the regulation of gene expression and the development of cancer.
the molecular mechanisms underlying the development of the prostate gland.
the role of microRNA in cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the embryonic prostate development program is a highly relevant source of genes, pathways, and functional themes for the study of prostate cancer.
early androgen-induced prostate development is an excellent model for human prostate carcinogenesis.
the embryonic development of the prostate is a valid model for prostate cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
early prostate development recapitulates the molecular program of human prostate cancer, which is a disease of reactivation.

the early androgen-regulation of the prostate epithelium recapitulates many of the molecular features of the prostate tumor microenvironment, and thus represents a useful model system for the identification and validation of genes and pathways relevant to prostate cancer progression.
early prostate development recapitulates prostate cancer, and that the early prostate program is reactivated during prostate cancer progression.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the prostate cancer gene expression profile is not random, but rather reflects an early androgen-regulation program that is reactivated during cancer progression.

the early androgen-regulation program in the prostate rudiment closely resembles the program in prostate cancer, and that this early program is a reliable model system for the study of prostate carcinogenesis and progression.
prostate cancer is not simply a disease that results from the accumulation of somatically acquired genetic changes in a prostate epithelium.
